name: Mfumte, Lus standard variety
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Eyoh, Julius A. and Robert Hedinger. 2008. Mfumte orthography guide. Yaoundé: National Association of Cameroonian Language Committees (NACALCO). iv+12 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives 32291; archived silcam.org PDF). Corroborating: McLean, Greg L. 2014. A Sketch Grammar of the Central Mfumte Language. Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon. 35 pp.
catalog_locator: Sec. 3 'Tones' and 3.1 'Lexical Contrasts Marked by Diacritics', pp. 8-9
catalog_quote: We have identified five surface tones in Mfumte: three level tones: high [á], mid [ā] and low [à]; and two contour tones, rising [ǎ] and falling [â]. ... As of this point in time, we have discovered many minimal tone pairs for words that contrast the level tones: high, mid and low with each other and we conclude that these three tones need to be clearly distinguished from each other. ... Though we have not found any tone pairs for rising tones against other tones among singular nouns, there are many nouns that only distinguish their plural forms by the root becoming rising. In addition, many verbs become rising in their hortative and imperative forms. ... We have only found two minimal noun pairs that contrast falling tone with high tone (and none with any other tone). Many of the falling tones are found in two easily identified environments: on the "prefix" /mâ-/ and on the second syllable with lots of reduplicated roots (precisely where falling tone contrasts with mid tone). ... Our proposal is to write all Mfumte words as they occur in isolation (i.e. as they occur when pronounced by themselves), and it is these forms that will be written in the lexicon.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Central Mfumte (Lus) is described as a tone language with three contrastive level tones (H, M, L) plus rising and falling contours, tone carrying both lexical and grammatical (plural, hortative/imperative) contrasts; neither this guide nor McLean's 2014 sketch grammar says anything about word stress or accent, so no stress position can be stated from accessible sources.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tone: rising tone mostly grammatical - noun plurals, hortatives/imperatives; falling tone concentrated on the prefix mâ- and second syllables of reduplicated roots, p. 9.)
new_statements.domain_note: Tone description refers to isolation (citation) forms: 'Our proposal is to write all Mfumte words as they occur in isolation' (p. 9). McLean 2014 p. 9 likewise uses surface tone only and adds a 'super high' surface tone in its conventions (p. 5). No statement at word or phrase level about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both held sources describe the variety of the village of Lus (Ndə'wuli'), which McLean 2014 explicitly calls 'Central Mfumte' (= Glottolog cent2312) and which Eyoh & Hedinger 2008 treat as the standard 'Mfumte' variety; both carry ISO nfu, which Glottolog now assigns to Southern Mfumte (mfum1238, Koffa etc.), so the ISO code alone would misfile them. Glottolog's own comment on cent2312 equates it with Ethnologue's 'Kwaja (kdz-NOCODE_Central-Mfumte)' entry.

sources.note: Nothing about stress or accent. Sec. 3 'Tones' pp. 8-10: five surface tones (high, mid, low level; rising, falling contour), many H/M/L minimal pairs, tone also marks noun plural and hortative/imperative; consonant/vowel phoneme charts pp. 2-8. Based on the Lus (standard) variety.
